Laguna San Rafael National Park lies in Chilean Patagonia, near the Northern Patagonian Ice Field. The glacier descends towards the lagoon, where pieces of ice that have broken away can be seen near its edge. Forested slopes and snow-covered mountains rise above the water.

The water route to this area passes through the Chonos Archipelago and the Moraleda Channel. On a cruise, visitors discover fjords, islands and coves, and view the glacier from the water.

San Rafael is a natural stop on an itinerary through the Chilean fjords: the main attraction here is the glacier and the remote coastal landscapes around it.

The path to Laime leads through tropical rainforest after disembarking at Ratoncito. Along the way are small streams, trees with orchids and bromeliads, and stones covered in green moss. At the end of the walk, Angel Falls comes into view, its long stream of water set against the cliffs.

The viewpoint is part of a one-day excursion to the waterfall. On this itinerary, the walk takes about an hour; after enjoying the view, guests have lunch and return to Canaima.

Lake Acajatuba is a place to explore the Amazon by boat. Dark water reflects the treetops, a dense wall of green forest reaches the shores, and narrow channels open out beyond broad stretches of water. The lake belongs to the Rio Negro river system near Manaus. Here, waterways connect the forest, small settlements and boat landings.

On a canoe outing, details that are easy to miss from a large riverboat come into focus: tangled roots, overhanging branches and birds moving above the shore. A local guide can help visitors distinguish the sounds of the forest and understand how the landscape changes around them. Water levels determine which channels and stretches of flooded forest can be reached, so the experience varies with the season.

In the Acajatuba area, igapó forests, which flood when the river rises, lie alongside terra firme woodland that remains above the water. Boat outings can be combined with walks on land if these are included in the chosen itinerary. Moving between these vantage points reveals more of the Amazon: first the reflections and riverside vegetation, then trunks, leaves and forest trails at close range.

Riverside communities add an insight into local life to the natural experience. Wooden homes, boats moored along the shore and residents' stories show the role the river plays in everyday routines. Lake Acajatuba will appeal to travelers who enjoy observing, listening and discovering a vast natural world through small details.

The lake's best-known natural attraction is the Perito Moreno Glacier, one of the few major glaciers in the region that continues to advance actively. Its majestic wall of ice drops directly into the lake, creating a striking contrast between the white-blue ice and the calm water.

Exploring the lake offers an entirely different perspective on Patagonia. Boat excursions take visitors close to glacier fronts, among icebergs, and offer views of enormous masses of ice rising above the water. Numerous birds live along the shores and on the islands, while the surrounding mountains form an impressive natural amphitheater.

Lake Argentino lies within Los Glaciares National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Together with glaciers, mountain valleys and Patagonian steppes, it forms one of the most recognizable landscapes of southern Argentina.

This place captures Patagonia particularly well: expansive, somewhat austere and extraordinarily beautiful. Distances seem endless here, mountains are reflected in the cold water, and ancient ice evokes the power of nature as it continues to shape the region.
